ai.definition: AI in drug discovery refers to the application of artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques to accelerate the identification and optimization of new drug compounds.
ai.howItWorks: Predictive algorithms analyze large datasets, including chemical structures, biological interactions, and clinical trial results, to identify potential drug candidates. These models can predict how a compound might interact with specific targets or pathways in the body, thereby streamlining the early stages of drug development.
ai.problemSolved: Traditional drug discovery methods are time-consuming and resource-intensive due to the need for extensive laboratory testing and animal studies. AI can significantly reduce this process by predicting which compounds are most likely to be effective before they enter expensive and lengthy clinical trials.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing of drugs using AI involves designing and optimizing production processes based on predictive models, but does not typically include the actual synthesis of drug compounds in early stages.
ai.buildProcess: AI models for drug discovery are built by training algorithms on large datasets. This includes chemical databases, genomic information, and existing clinical trial data. The process requires significant computational resources and expertise in both AI and pharmaceuticals.
ai.costDrivers: High costs associated with data acquisition, model development, and validation. Additionally, the need for powerful computing infrastructure to run complex machine learning algorithms.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is rapidly advancing and showing promising results in early-stage drug discovery, but widespread adoption faces regulatory hurdles and requires further validation through clinical trials.
ai.regulation: Current regulations require extensive testing of drugs before approval. AI-driven drug candidates must still undergo rigorous safety and efficacy evaluations to meet regulatory standards.
ai.risks: Risks include over-reliance on predictive models that may not fully capture all complexities of biological systems, potential legal issues related to data privacy and intellectual property, and the challenge of translating model predictions into effective clinical treatments.
ai.profitability: While AI in drug discovery has the potential for significant cost savings and faster time-to-market, profitability is highly dependent on successful validation through clinical trials and regulatory approval processes.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on improving model accuracy, expanding datasets to include more diverse biological information, and integrating AI with other technologies such as CRISPR and synthetic biology.

glossary.def: A subset of artificial intelligence that involves training algorithms to make predictions or decisions without being explicitly programmed.
The use of computer simulations and mathematical models to study the properties of chemical systems, often used in drug discovery to predict molecular behavior.
The process by which a government agency evaluates new drugs for safety and efficacy before granting permission for their sale and distribution.

subsystems.name: Data layer
subsystems.role: collects and standardises the biological, chemical and clinical data that models learn from.
parts: public protein structure and sequence databases

subsystems.name: Target discovery models
subsystems.role: identify and prioritise disease-causing proteins or pathways.
parts: knowledge graphs linking genes to disease

subsystems.name: Structure and binding models
subsystems.role: predict the 3D shapes of targets and how candidate molecules bind to them.

subsystems.name: Generative chemistry models
subsystems.role: propose novel molecules with desired properties.
parts: variational autoencoders, GANs or diffusion models

subsystems.name: Property and safety predictors
subsystems.role: estimate absorption, toxicity, metabolism and other drug-like qualities before synthesis.

subsystems.name: Experimental validation loop
subsystems.role: tests AI predictions in the lab and feeds results back to improve the models.

buildSteps.title: Curate the data
buildSteps.detail: Gather and clean bioactivity, structural, genomic and clinical data; standardise chemical structures and assay results so models can learn from them.

buildSteps.title: Train predictive models
buildSteps.detail: Train or fine-tune machine-learning models to predict protein structure, binding affinity, toxicity and other properties from sequence and chemical structure.

buildSteps.title: Choose and validate a target
buildSteps.detail: Use genomics and AI prioritisation to pick a protein implicated in disease, then confirm its role with lab experiments such as CRISPR knockouts.

buildSteps.title: Generate candidate molecules
buildSteps.detail: Generative models propose novel molecules that fit the target; filters remove those that are impossible to make or too similar to known compounds.

buildSteps.title: Predict and rank
buildSteps.detail: Models estimate potency, selectivity, ADMET properties and safety; docking simulates how each candidate binds. Only the top-ranked few move forward.

buildSteps.title: Synthesise and assay
buildSteps.detail: Top candidates are made, often with automated synthesis, and tested in high-throughput biochemical and cell assays.

buildSteps.title: Learn from results
buildSteps.detail: Assay data feeds back to retrain the models, and the design–make–test–analyse cycle repeats, improving predictions each round.

buildSteps.title: Advance to trials
buildSteps.detail: Optimised candidates undergo animal testing, then phased human trials; AI helps design trials and analyse the resulting data.

prerequisites.why: many public and proprietary datasets exist, but they are fragmented, biased and often not machine-readable.
AlphaFold and similar tools predict many single-protein structures accurately, but not all complexes, motions or binding affinities.
training and running these models needs GPUs and large storage, now widely available.
robotic labs can run thousands of assays, but closed-loop integration with AI is still rare.

prerequisites.tech: Regulatory frameworks for AI in medicine
prerequisites.why: regulators are issuing guidance, but standards for AI-derived evidence and model transparency are still evolving.

pathway.milestone: AI models routinely predict protein structures and screen billions of compounds virtually
pathway.unlocks: faster hit finding and repurposing of existing drugs.

pathway.milestone: first AI-designed drugs complete late-stage trials and reach approval
pathway.unlocks: validation of the whole approach and investment at scale.

pathway.milestone: closed-loop autonomous labs run design–make–test–analyse cycles with minimal human input
pathway.unlocks: discovery timelines cut from years to months.

pathway.milestone: generative models design new proteins, enzymes and cell therapies for previously undruggable targets
pathway.unlocks: treatments for diseases that have resisted small-molecule drugs.
